hello.title: Hello, Scala
hello.summary: Write your first Scala program, print text with println and print, and join strings.
hello.lesson.0: Every Scala program needs a starting point. The line `@main def run(): Unit =` creates it. `def` defines a function, `run` is its name, the empty parentheses `()` mean it takes no input, `: Unit` means it gives back no useful value, and `=` says that the body follows. `@main` marks this function as the place where the program starts.
hello.lesson.2: The body is the indented code below the first line. `println` prints the text in the parentheses and then starts a new line. Text in double quotes, like `"Hello, Scala!"`, is called a **string**. Each `println` prints its own line, from top to bottom.
hello.lesson.5: `print` works like `println`, but it does not start a new line. The next output continues on the same line. `println()` with nothing in the parentheses only starts a new line.
hello.lesson.7: Numbers are written without quotes, and Scala can calculate with them: `2 + 3` gives `5`. Inside quotes, `"2 + 3"` is only text and is printed as it is. With strings, `+` joins them into one string.
hello.lesson.9: Scala 3 uses indentation to group code. All lines of the body must start with the same number of spaces. Two spaces is the usual style. Older Scala code puts the body in curly braces `{` and `}` instead.
hello.lesson.10: Scala is case-sensitive: `println` works, but `Println` or `PrintLn` is an error. A string also needs a double quote at the start and at the end.
hello.card.0: `@main def run(): Unit =` starts the program
hello.card.4: Indent the body, usually by 2 spaces
hello-1.prompt: Which line prints Hello on its own line?
hello-1.explain: `println` prints the string in the parentheses and then starts a new line. The other commands do not exist in Scala.
hello-2.explain: `print` does not start a new line, so all three parts end up on one line: `Scala!`.
hello-3.explain: Without quotes, `6 * 7` is a calculation. `*` multiplies, so Scala prints `42`.
hello-4.explain: The calculation is inside double quotes, so it is only text. The program prints `3 + 4`.
hello-5.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints Hi and Bye on two lines.
hello-5.explain: `println` starts a new line after `Hi`. With `print`, the output would be `HiBye`.
hello-6.prompt: Fill the gap to define the starting point of the program.
hello-6.explain: In Scala, functions are defined with `def`. `fun` and `func` are keywords of other languages.
hello-7.prompt: Build a line that prints the sum of 2 and 3.
hello-7.explain: `println( 2 + 3 )` calculates `2 + 3` and prints `5`. Spaces next to the parentheses do not matter.
hello-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints One, Two and Three on separate lines.
hello-8.explain: The program starts with `@main def run(): Unit =`. The `println` lines run from top to bottom.
hello-9.prompt: Match each piece of code with its meaning.
hello-9.pairs.0: prints Hi and starts a new line
hello-9.pairs.1: prints Hi without a new line
hello-10.explain: The string `"Middle` has no closing double quote. Correct: `println("Middle")`.
hello-11.explain: Scala is case-sensitive. `Println` does not exist; write `println("Bye")`.
hello-12.prompt: In `@main def run(): Unit =`, what does `Unit` mean?
hello-12.options.0: The function gives back no useful value
hello-12.options.1: The function gives back a number
hello-12.explain: The type after the colon is the type of the result. `Unit` means that there is no useful result: `run` only does something, like printing.
values.title: Values and types
values.summary: Store data with val and var, and get to know Int, Double, Boolean, String and type inference.
values.lesson.0: A **value** gives a name to a piece of data. You write `val`, the name, `=` and the data. After that, you can use the name instead of the data. A `val` can never change.
values.lesson.2: When something needs to change, use `var` for a **variable**. You give it a new value with `=`. `score += 5` is short for `score = score + 5`; `-=` and `*=` work the same way.
values.lesson.4: Giving a `val` a new value is an error: the program does not compile and Scala reports `Reassignment to val`. Use `val` by default and `var` only when the value really has to change.
values.lesson.6: Every value has a **type**. `Int` is a whole number, `Double` is a number with decimals, `Boolean` is `true` or `false`, and `String` is text. Usually Scala works out the type by itself; this is called **type inference**. You can also write the type after a colon: `val age: Int = 25`.
values.lesson.8: Scala calculates with `+`, `-`, `*` (multiply) and `/` (divide). `%` gives the remainder of a division. Be careful: when you divide two `Int` values, the result is an `Int` too, and the decimals are cut off. If one of the numbers is a `Double`, the result has decimals.
values.lesson.10: To change the type of a value, use a conversion: `toDouble` turns a number into a `Double`, `toInt` turns a `Double` into an `Int` and cuts off the decimals, and `toInt` on a string like `"42"` reads the number in it.
values.lesson.12: A type mismatch is an error. `val age: Int = "25"` does not compile, because `"25"` is a `String`, not an `Int`. Scala finds such mistakes before the program runs.
values-1.prompt: Which keyword creates a variable that you can change later?
values-1.explain: A `var` can get a new value with `=`. A `val` can never change.
values-2.explain: Both numbers are `Int` values, so the result is an `Int`. `17 / 5` is `3.4`, and the decimals are cut off: `3`.
values-3.explain: `%` gives the remainder. `5` fits into `17` three times (`15`), and `2` is left over.
values-4.explain: `b` starts as `10` and becomes `15`. `a` stays `10`. `10 + 15` is `25`.
values-5.explain: `n` is a `val`, so it cannot get a new value. The program does not compile. With `var n = 5` it would print `6`.
values-6.prompt: Fill the gap with the right type.
values-6.explain: `4.5` has decimals, so its type is `Double`. An `Int` can only hold whole numbers.
values-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints 3.
values-7.explain: `count += 2` adds `2` to `count`, so it becomes `3`. `count = 2` would set it to `2`, and `==` only compares.
values-8.prompt: Create a value named age of type Int with the value 30 that can never change.
values-8.explain: `val age: Int = 30` creates a value that cannot change. The type comes after the colon and starts with a capital letter.
values-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 12.
values-9.explain: `total` starts at `2`, `2 * 3` is `6`, and `6 + 6` is `12`. In the other order, `(2 + 6) * 3` would be `24`.
values-10.explain: `"25"` is a `String`, but `age` must be an `Int`. Write the number without quotes: `val age: Int = 25`.
values-11.explain: `price` is a `Double`, and Scala does not turn it into an `Int` by itself. Convert it: `val whole: Int = price.toInt`.
values-12.prompt: Match each type with the kind of data it holds.
strings.title: Strings
strings.summary: Build text with s-interpolation and use length, toUpperCase, contains and substring.
strings.lesson.0: A `String` is text in double quotes. You already know that `+` joins strings. When you join a string and a number, Scala turns the number into text: `"Age: " + 36` gives `"Age: 36"`.
strings.lesson.3: An easier way to build text is **string interpolation**. Write the letter `s` right before the opening quote. Inside the string, `$name` puts in the value of `name`. For a calculation or a longer expression, use curly braces: `${age + 1}`.
strings.lesson.5: Do not forget the `s` before the quote. Without it, Scala prints `$name` as plain text and does not put in the value.
strings.lesson.7: Strings have many **methods**: functions that belong to a value. You call them with a dot after the value. `length` counts the characters, `toUpperCase` and `toLowerCase` change capital letters, and `contains` checks if a text is inside the string. `contains` gives a `Boolean`.
strings.lesson.9: Every character in a string has a position, called its **index**. The first character has index `0`. `substring(start, end)` gives the characters from index `start` up to, but not including, index `end`. `substring(start)` goes to the end of the string. `replace` swaps one text for another.
strings.lesson.11: A string never changes. Methods like `toUpperCase` give back a **new** string, and the original string stays the same. To keep the result, store it in a new `val`.
strings-1.explain: Because of the `s` before the quote, `$name` is replaced by the value `Eva`.
strings-2.explain: `length` counts the characters: b, a, n, a, n, a. That is `6`.
strings-3.explain: `substring(0, 3)` takes the characters with index `0`, `1` and `2`. The character at index `3` is not included.
strings-4.explain: `$a` and `$b` put in the values `4` and `3`. `${a + b}` calculates first and puts in `7`. The `+` outside the braces is plain text.
strings-5.explain: The string has no `s` before the quote, so `$name` stays plain text. The program prints `Hello, $name`.
strings-6.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints ANA.
strings-6.explain: `toUpperCase` gives back the string with capital letters: `ANA`.
strings-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints I live in Paris.
strings-7.explain: The letter `s` right before the quote turns on string interpolation, so `$city` becomes `Paris`.
strings-8.prompt: Build a line that stores word in capital letters in a new value named upper.
strings-8.explain: Methods are called with a dot after the value: `word.toUpperCase`. The result is stored in `upper`.
strings-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints SCALA has 5 letters.
strings-9.explain: Each line uses the value from the line before it: `lang`, then `big`, then `count`. A value must exist before you can use it.
strings-10.prompt: Match each piece of code with what it does.
strings-10.pairs.0: puts a value into a string
strings-10.pairs.2: gives the text in capital letters
strings-10.pairs.3: checks if a text is inside
strings-10.pairs.4: gives a part of the text
strings-11.explain: The last string has no `s` before the quote, so `${first.length}` is printed as plain text. Correct: `println(s"Letters: ${first.length}")`.
strings-12.explain: Method names are case-sensitive. The method is called `toUpperCase`, with a capital `C`.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Make decisions with if, then and else, compare and combine conditions, and choose with match.
conditions.lesson.0: A comparison gives a `Boolean`: `true` or `false`. Scala has `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<` (less than), `>` (greater than), `<=` (less than or equal) and `>=` (greater than or equal). You can compare strings with `==` too.
conditions.lesson.2: `if` runs code only when a condition is `true`. Write `if`, the condition, `then`, and the code below it, indented. The `else` part is optional: it runs when the condition is `false`.
conditions.lesson.4: With `else if` you can check more conditions, one after the other. Scala runs the code of the first condition that is `true` and skips the rest.
conditions.lesson.6: In Scala, `if` is an **expression**: it gives back a value. You can store this value in a `val`. Short ones fit on one line: `if a > b then a else b` gives `a` when `a` is bigger, otherwise `b`.
conditions.lesson.8: **Logical operators** combine conditions. `&&` (and) is `true` when both sides are true. `||` (or) is `true` when at least one side is true. `!` (not) turns `true` into `false` and `false` into `true`.
conditions.lesson.11: `match` compares one value with several patterns. Each `case` has a pattern, an arrow `=>` and a result. Scala checks the cases from top to bottom and takes the first one that fits. `|` puts several values into one case, and `_` fits every value, so it goes last. Like `if`, `match` gives back a value.
conditions.lesson.13: In the second `match`, `case x if x > 0` gives the value the name `x` and adds a condition, called a **guard**. The case fits only when the guard is `true`.
conditions.card.2: `val max = if a > b then a else b`
conditions-1.explain: `7 > 5` is `true`, so the code after `then` runs.
conditions-2.explain: `9 % 2` is `1`, not `0`. The condition is `false`, so `if` gives back `"odd"`.
conditions-3.explain: The case `2 | 3` fits both `2` and `3`, so `text` is `"few"`.
conditions-4.explain: `!=` means "not equal". `5` is equal to `5`, so the result is `false`.
conditions-5.explain: `a > 2` is `true`, but `b < 5` is `false`. With `&&`, both sides must be true, so it prints `false`.
conditions-6.prompt: Fill the gap so that both conditions must be true to get in.
conditions-6.explain: `&&` needs both sides to be true. Here `age >= 18` is `false`, so the program prints `Sorry`. With `||`, the member would get in although `age` is only `15`.
conditions-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints large.
conditions-7.explain: The form is `if condition then a else b`. Here `n > 10` is `true`, so `size` is `"large"`.
conditions-8.prompt: Build a line that stores the smaller of a and b in min.
conditions-8.explain: `if a < b then a else b` gives back `a` when it is smaller, otherwise `b`.
conditions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints Grade B.
conditions-9.explain: `75 >= 90` is `false`, so the `else` part runs. It must contain `println("Grade B")`.
conditions-10.prompt: Match each operator with its meaning.
conditions-10.pairs.1: or: at least one must be true
conditions-11.explain: A single `=` gives a name a value. To compare, write `==`: `if age == 18 then`.
conditions-12.explain: In a `case`, the pattern and the result are separated by `=>`, not `->`. Correct: `case _ => "many"`.
loops.title: Loops and ranges
loops.summary: Repeat code with for and while, count with ranges like 1 to 5, and build new collections with yield.
loops.lesson.0: A `for` loop repeats code. `1 to 3` is a **range**: the numbers `1`, `2` and `3`, including the last one. In `for i <- 1 to 3 do`, the arrow `<-` takes each number from the range, one after the other, and gives it the name `i`. The code after `do` runs once for each number.
loops.lesson.2: `until` makes a range **without** the last number: `0 until 3` is `0`, `1` and `2`. With `by` you choose the step: `1 to 10 by 3` counts `1`, `4`, `7`, `10`. A short loop body can stay on the same line as `do`.
loops.lesson.4: To collect a result, create a `var` before the loop and change it inside the loop. Here `total` adds up the numbers from `1` to `4`.
loops.lesson.7: A `while` loop repeats its code as long as a condition is `true`. Scala checks the condition before every round. Inside the loop, you must change something so that the condition becomes `false` one day. `count -= 1` makes `count` one smaller.
loops.lesson.9: If the condition of a `while` loop never becomes `false`, the loop never ends. Check that the loop changes the variable in the condition.
loops.lesson.11: With `yield` instead of `do`, a `for` loop does not run code but builds a **new collection**: one result for each value. For a range, the result is a `Vector`, a collection that holds values in order. `println` shows it as `Vector(…)`.
loops.lesson.13: To count down, use a negative step: `for i <- 3 to 1 by -1 do` counts `3`, `2`, `1`. A range like `3 to 1` without a step is empty, so the loop does not run at all.
loops.card.2: `1 to 10 by 2` counts in steps of 2
loops-1.explain: `1 to 4` includes `4`. `print` does not start a new line, so the numbers end up next to each other.
loops-3.explain: `0 until 3` starts at `0` and stops before `3`: `0`, `1`, `2`.
loops-4.explain: `n` goes from `10` to `5`, then `2`, then `1`. Now `n > 1` is `false`. That makes `3` rounds.
loops-5.statement: `1 to 5` and `1 until 5` contain the same numbers.
loops-5.explain: `1 to 5` includes `5`: `1` to `5`. `1 until 5` stops before `5`: `1` to `4`.
loops-6.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints 1, 2 and 3 on separate lines.
loops-6.explain: `1 to 3` includes the last number. `1 until 3` would stop after `2`.
loops-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints Vector(2, 4, 6).
loops-7.explain: `yield` builds a new collection from the results. With `do`, the loop only runs code and gives back no collection.
loops-8.prompt: Build a loop that prints the numbers 0 to 4.
loops-8.explain: `0 until 5` gives `0` to `4`. The arrow `<-` takes each number, and the code after `do` prints it.
loops-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 3, 2 and 1 on separate lines.
loops-9.explain: The loop must print `n` first and then make it smaller. In the other order it would print `2`, `1`, `0`.
loops-10.prompt: Match each range with its numbers.
loops-11.explain: In a `for` loop, the arrow that takes each value is `<-`, not `->`. Correct: `for i <- 1 to 3 do`.
loops-12.prompt: The program should print Line 1, Line 2 and Line 3. Which line has the bug?
loops-12.explain: `1 until 3` stops before `3`, so the program prints only two lines. Use `1 to 3` to include `3`.
functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Write your own functions with def, parameters and return types, use default arguments and lambdas.
functions.lesson.0: A **function** is a piece of code with a name that you can use again and again. You define it with `def`, the name, the **parameters** in parentheses and the return type after a colon. Every parameter needs a type. The value of the code after `=` is the result; you do not need a `return` keyword.
functions.lesson.2: Parameters are separated by commas. When you call the function, the **arguments** go into the parameters in the same order. A body with several lines is indented, and the last line gives the result.
functions.lesson.4: A function that only does something, like printing, has the return type `Unit`. You call it on its own line.
functions.lesson.6: A parameter can have a **default value**, written with `=` in the parameter list. When you leave out that argument, Scala uses the default. With **named arguments** like `greeting = "Hey"`, you say which parameter gets which value, in any order.
functions.lesson.9: A **lambda** is a function without a name. `(x: Int) => x * 2` takes `x` and gives back `x * 2`. The arrow `=>` separates the parameters from the result. You can store a lambda in a `val` and call it like any function. Its type is written `Int => Int`: it takes an `Int` and gives back an `Int`.
functions.lesson.11: A function can take another function as a parameter. `applyTwice` below calls `f` two times. You can pass a stored lambda or write a new one directly in the call. In the call, `x => x + 10` needs no type, because Scala knows that `f` takes an `Int`.
functions.lesson.13: Scala can often work out the return type by itself, so `def square(n: Int) = n * n` also works. Writing the return type makes your code easier to read and helps the compiler find mistakes.
functions.card.1: The last expression is the result
functions.card.2: `def f(x: Int = 1)` has a default value
functions.card.4: `Unit`: the function gives back nothing useful
functions-2.explain: The call leaves out `age`, so Scala uses the default value `30`.
functions-3.explain: `c` is `2 + 3`, which is `5`. The last line `c * 2` is the result: `10`.
functions-4.prompt: Which line correctly defines a function that adds two `Int` values?
functions-4.options.0: `def add(a: Int, b: Int): Int = a + b`
functions-4.options.2: `fun add(a: Int, b: Int): Int = a + b`
functions-4.options.3: `def add(a: Int, b: Int): Int => a + b`
functions-4.explain: A Scala function starts with `def`, every parameter needs a type, and the body comes after `=`. `fun` is Kotlin, and `=>` is used for lambdas.
functions-5.statement: A Scala function needs the keyword `return` to give back a value.
functions-5.explain: The value of the body is the result. In a body with several lines, the last line is the result. `return` is not needed.
functions-6.prompt: Fill the gap with the right return type.
functions-6.explain: `n % 2 == 0` is a comparison, so the result is `true` or `false`: a `Boolean`.
functions-7.prompt: Fill the gap to complete the lambda.
functions-7.explain: In a lambda, `=>` separates the parameters from the result. `half(9)` gives `4.5`.
functions-8.prompt: Build a function cube that gives back n * n * n.
functions-8.explain: `def cube(n: Int): Int = n * n * n` has a name, a parameter with a type, a return type and the body after `=`.
functions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the function gives back the price plus tax.
functions-9.explain: The function header comes first. `extra` must exist before `total` uses it, and the last line `total` is the result.
functions-10.prompt: Match each piece of code with its meaning.
functions-10.pairs.3: a parameter with a default value
functions-11.explain: `greet` has one parameter, but the call passes two arguments. Correct: `println(greet("Ana"))`.
functions-12.explain: Every parameter needs a type. Correct: `def add(a: Int, b: Int): Int =`.
collections.title: Lists and maps
collections.summary: Keep many values in a List or a Map, and work with them using map, filter, sum and foreach.
collections.lesson.0: A `List` holds several values in a fixed order. You create it with `List(…)` and the values separated by commas. `fruits(0)` gives the element at index `0`, the first one. `length` counts the elements, and `contains` checks if a value is in the list.
collections.lesson.2: A list never changes. `:+` gives back a **new** list with one more element at the end; the old list stays the same. With a `for` loop, you can go through all elements of a list.
collections.lesson.4: `map` uses a function on every element and gives back a new list with the results. `filter` keeps only the elements for which the function gives `true`. `sum` adds all numbers. Instead of `x => x + 1`, you can write `_ + 1`: the `_` stands for the element.
collections.lesson.6: You can call several methods one after the other. `foreach` runs a function for every element, for example `println`. `mkString` joins all elements into one string, with the text you give between them.
collections.lesson.9: A `Map` stores pairs of a **key** and a **value**. `"Ana" -> 31` makes a pair with the key `"Ana"` and the value `31`. `ages("Ana")` gives the value for a key. `getOrElse` gives a default value when the key is missing. `+` gives back a new map with one more pair, and `size` counts the pairs.
collections.lesson.11: A `for` loop can go through a map, too. In `for (fruit, count) <- stock do`, each pair is split into two names: `fruit` for the key and `count` for the value.
collections.lesson.13: `ages("Zoe")` stops the program with an error when the key `"Zoe"` is missing. Use `getOrElse` when you are not sure that a key exists.
collections-1.explain: The index starts at `0`. `nums(0)` is `4`, so `nums(1)` is `8`.
collections-3.explain: `filter` keeps the elements for which `_ > 4` is `true`: `5`, `12` and `20`.
collections-4.options.3: Nothing, the program stops with an error
collections-4.explain: The key `"Eva"` is missing, so `getOrElse` gives back the default value `-1`.
collections-5.explain: `:+` gives back a new list, which is stored in `b`. The list `a` does not change, so the program prints `List(1, 2)`.
collections-6.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints List(HI, YO).
collections-6.explain: `map` uses the function on every element and gives back a new list with the results.
collections-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints List(8, 6).
collections-7.explain: Only `8` and `6` are greater than `5`, so `filter(_ > 5)` keeps them.
collections-8.prompt: Build a line that keeps only the even numbers of nums.
collections-8.explain: `filter` keeps the elements for which the condition is `true`. `_ % 2 == 0` is `true` for even numbers.
collections-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 12.
collections-9.explain: `small` is `List(1, 2, 3)`, `doubled` is `List(2, 4, 6)`, and the sum is `12`. Each line needs the value from the line before.
collections-10.prompt: Match each method with what it does.
collections-10.pairs.4: gives a default when a key is missing
collections-11.explain: To add an element at the end of a list, use `:+`: `val more = fruits :+ "kiwi"`.
collections-12.prompt: The program should print 3 and then 0. Which line has the bug?
collections-12.explain: The key `"coffee"` is missing, so `stock("coffee")` stops the program with an error. Use `stock.getOrElse("coffee", 0)`.
classes.title: Case classes and Option
classes.summary: Group data in case classes, add methods, take values apart with match, and handle missing values with Option.
classes.lesson.0: A **case class** groups values that belong together into a new type. `case class Point(x: Int, y: Int)` defines a type `Point` with two **fields**, `x` and `y`. You create a point with `Point(3, 4)` and read a field with a dot: `p.x`. `println` shows the class name and the values.
classes.lesson.2: The fields of a case class cannot change. `copy` gives back a new object with some fields changed; the others keep their values. `==` compares two case class objects by their values.
classes.lesson.4: A case class can have **methods**: functions that belong to it. Put a colon after the class header and write the methods below it, indented. Methods can use the fields directly. A method without parameters, like `area`, needs no parentheses.
classes.lesson.6: `match` can take a case class apart. `case Point(0, 0)` fits only when both fields are `0`. `case Point(x, 0)` fits when `y` is `0` and gives the first field the name `x`. `_` fits any value.
classes.lesson.9: Sometimes a value can be missing. An `Option[Int]` is either `Some(value)`, when there is an `Int`, or `None`, when there is nothing. The type in square brackets says what the `Option` can hold. `find` gives back the first element that fits, as an `Option`. `getOrElse` gives the value inside, or a default for `None`.
classes.lesson.11: You can use `match` on an `Option`, too. `case Some(v)` fits when there is a value and gives it the name `v`. `case None` fits when the value is missing.
classes.lesson.13: When a function gives back an `Option`, its type tells you that the value can be missing. You cannot use an `Option[Int]` like an `Int`; you must first handle both cases, for example with `getOrElse` or `match`. This prevents many errors.
classes-1.explain: `b.pages` reads the field `pages` of the book, which is `412`.
